units: a sky seen from a lit street looks almost emptied out
on a remote plateau the same vault shows a swarm of stars
the whitish band then runs across the sky from one edge to the other
the watcher also picks out different tints among the stars
the gap between the two skies comes from the background, not the equipment
the glow of street lighting wipes out the faintest objects
high up, the dry air darkens the background of the sky
enthusiasts travel long distances to find darkness
text: Look up from a lit street and you would swear the sky had been emptied out. A dozen pale specks, a smear you half imagine, and that is your lot. Take the same pair of eyes up to a bare plateau, well away from the lamps, and the whole vault swarms. Specks everywhere, and that milky band running clean across from one edge to the other. Give it a while and you start catching colours too, one star coppery, the next faintly blue. None of that is down to your kit. It is down to the background. Below, the glow off the lamps drowns the frailest things and leaves a grey mush behind them. High up, the dry air turns that background nearly black, so every small spark stands out. That is why enthusiasts drive for hours before setting up a tripod. They are not chasing a better telescope, they are chasing a better dark.

units: the writer refuses to have near orbit treated as a rubbish tip
he sets out three sides of the problem
launcher parts left in place endanger craft still working
highly reflective satellites spoil astronomical images
no operator carries the cost of clearing up
the usual objection appeals to the vastness of the void
the writer answers that the paths in use are narrow and overloaded
he concludes that shared regulation is missing
text: We ought to stop treating low orbit as a rubbish tip that nobody minds. Anyone willing to look squarely at it runs into three separate matters. The first is debris: every spent rocket stage left up there turns into a projectile aimed at craft still doing their job. The second falls on observing from the ground, where strings of glaring satellites streak across telescope plates and wreck whole measuring campaigns. The third gets the least airing, and it concerns who pays. No operator picks up the bill for the clearing-up it forces on whoever comes later. The stock reply is that space is enormous, dizzyingly so, and that the danger looks slight. That reply collapses once you look at the corridors actually in use, which are narrow and crammed. A cluttered orbit is no matter for engineers. It calls for rules held in common, and those are what we lack.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: as a small child she watched the sky from the roof of her parents' farm
she wrote her observations down in a notebook
as a teenager she built an instrument herself from cardboard and salvaged lenses
the image she got was unsteady and far from sharp, which contented her
she was then taken on as an assistant at a high-altitude observatory
she recorded where the comets stood through whole nights
once she headed the survey, she spotted an unknown moving body
she refused to let that object carry her family name
at the end of her career she urged novices to set down what is real rather than what is expected
text: As a small girl she would climb onto the flat roof of her parents' farm to follow one distant star, a notebook balanced on her knees. In her teens she built a telescope of her own from a cardboard tube and two lenses rescued from a glazier's workshop. The image wobbled, it was never sharp, and that suited her. Taken on later as an assistant at a mountain observatory, she spent whole nights under a freezing sky noting where the comets stood. Once she was running the survey herself, she picked out something nobody had reported, a faint dot that shifted from one night to the next. She would never let it carry her family name. Towards the end of her working life she was still giving beginners a single rule, which she thought quite enough: draw what is there, not what you were hoping to find.

units: the reviewer judges the mechanical design of the device faulty
the main mirror is held at three points only
this mounting warps the mirror and makes the test star look stretched

that heat sets up air movements which spoil the image at high magnification
the electronics box lets in the damp of the night
the damp attacks the electrical contacts
the faults pile up and drop the device to the rank of a beginner's model
the remedies put forward are inexpensive
text: The way this telescope for amateurs is put together deserves a hard look, because its mechanical choices set off one failure after another. The primary mirror rests on three pads and no more; under its own weight it sags a little, and the test star spreads into an oval smudge instead of a clean disc. The tube, rolled from thin sheet metal, carries heat from the mount towards the optical axis, which keeps currents of air stirring inside and blurs the view at high magnification. The electronics box shuts badly and lets in the damp of the night, which in time eats away at the contacts. Any one of these faults could be lived with. Together they drag a scope sold as a performer down to the level of a starter model. Putting it right costs little: a nine-point cell, lagging on the tube, a seal on the box.

units: the request is made on behalf of an astronomy club
new lighting has been put up along the road bordering their site

text: I am writing to you on behalf of the observing society based on the plateau. Since the lighting recently put up along the road that skirts our field went into service, our sessions have become something of a trial. Part of the output from those lamps goes straight upwards, and the glare it makes hides everything faint from us. Members are losing heart, and the workshops we run for newcomers are being called off one after another. We are not asking for the road to be plunged back into darkness. There is a remedy, already in use elsewhere: fit each lamp with a hood that throws the light down onto the ground, then drop the power in the deepest part of the night. The outlay stays small, the bill falls, and the road loses none of its safety. We would gladly show you the trouble ourselves, on site, after dark.

units: a rocky planet offers hard ground where a craft can land
a gaseous planet presents nothing but a continuous sinking towards denser layers
the gas giants are markedly bulkier than the solid planets
their great mass lets them keep a thick gaseous envelope
a rocky body would not hold on to that envelope
both kinds form in the same starting disc
far from the star the cold packs ice together and forms massive cores
those cores then pull in the gas around them
bare ground throws back a sharp glint whereas an atmosphere spreads a soft striped light
text: What sets a rocky planet apart from a gaseous one? The first has a solid, rough surface that a craft could actually come down on and rest upon. The second offers nothing but an endless sinking through layers that grow denser and denser. Are the two of them much alike in size? Not at all: the gas giants dwarf the solid worlds by a wide margin, and their crushing mass holds on to a thick atmosphere that the pull of a rocky ball would simply let slip away. And where does each of them come from? Both kinds take shape within the same starting disc, but far out from the star the cold welds ice together, which yields cores heavy enough to draw in the gas around them. Do we observe them in the same way? Not quite: bare ground throws back a hard glint, while a gaseous envelope spreads a milky light in which bands can be made out.

units: the guide announces from the outset a session unlike an ordinary screening

the audience listens without stirring
text: The guide warned us at the door that this would be nothing like an ordinary screening. He began with the stars themselves: forget the idea of a fixed dot, he said, and picture a ball of gas burning itself away. Then he moved on to distances. One of the group asked whether the nearest star can be seen at all; he said it can, but that its light takes more than four years to reach us. After that came the instruments, from the wooden tubes of the early days to the mirrors we have now. He paused on the dark patches on the face of the sun and told us never to aim at it without a filter, or we would burn our eyes. He ended with the probes, craft sent off towards something far away that they never come back from. The oldest of them, he added, is still rolling through the void, well beyond the planets on our lists. Nobody in the room stirred.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before the first telescopes, the sky was charted without any optical instrument
the positions of the bright stars were set down in tables

photography made it possible to record stars invisible to the eye

electronic detectors turn out inventories too vast for a single team
text: Long before anyone thought of a telescope, watchers were already drawing charts of the sky with the naked eye, setting down in tables where the brightest stars stood. Those records steered ships and carved up the year. Then came the age of glass instruments, and the vault filled with objects nobody had suspected, spots and rings and moons. The catalogues swelled, and the trade changed character, since measuring now mattered as much as describing. The photographic plate tipped the discipline over altogether: a long exposure brought out stars far too frail for the eye, and charts stopped being drawn by hand. Later still, electronic detectors and automated surveys turn out inventories so vast that no single team could ever work through them. The vault overhead has not changed. What has changed is how we write it down.

units: the twinkling does not originate in the stars themselves
it happens in the atmosphere lying above the watcher
layers of air at different temperatures mix there without pause
each layer bends the beam that passes through it
the shifting path gives an impression of wavering and of changing tint
a planet shows a small disc rather than a single point
the rays from that disc cancel one another out and the light looks steady
watchers draw from this a way of telling a near body from a distant one
still air makes the finest detail visible
astronomers wait for those steady moments to record their images
text: That shivering we lay at the door of the stars is not theirs at all. It happens in the air we breathe, high above our heads. Warm and cold masses of it mingle up there without pause, and each one bends the beam that passes through, much as a flawed pane of glass would. The ray reaches us by a path that keeps shifting, so the star seems to tremble, to change its light, to turn coppery and then blue. A planet shows a tiny disc rather than a single point: its many rays cancel one another out, and its glow holds steady. From that watchers draw a rule, that what twinkles lies far off and what burns without a quiver is near. When the air settles, the vault sharpens and the finest detail that all the churning had rubbed away comes through at last; astronomers wait for those lulls and open the shutter exactly then.

units: the drive mechanism breaks down during a run of exposures

the repair would have taken a week, which the passage of the hairy star did not allow
the team shortens each exposure and then adds the frames together by computer
the outcome, less precise, still allows the movement of the body to be measured
text: The night looked superb right up to the moment the drive motor gave out, halfway through a run of exposures. With nothing driving it, the tube no longer held against the turning of our own world, and every frame came back streaked instead of pinpointed. The person running the dome suspected the power supply first, then put a meter on it: the voltage was fine. The fault lay in a pinion whose teeth had worn down until they slipped under load. A replacement part meant a week of waiting, and the passing of the hairy star was not going to wait. So the team cut each exposure to what the mount could hold without visible drift, and stacked the frames afterwards by computer. The outcome was coarser than they had hoped, but it served to measure how the nucleus moved. The lesson fitted in a line: a mechanical failure can be worked round in software too.
